The park mains hold water all winter at very low turnover, and spring temperatures warm the shallow lines quickly.
A full park flush at opening brings entrance quality water to the far end within a day.
In a year when the flush was skipped, complaints lasted three weeks; in flush years they end within days.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The town feed to the park is failing each spring
Water that sat in the park mains all winter is aged and depleted, and only flushing or weeks of use replace it
The park storage tank is contaminating the spring water
Spring runoff is entering the park mains

inference.explanation: Entrance water is strong on opening day, the far end improves exactly with use or flushing, and flush years end complaints in days while a skipped year lasted three weeks. The aged winter water in the park own mains explains it all; the park has no storage tank in this system, and runoff entry would threaten bacteriological results, which pass.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Make a full park flush and residual check part of the spring opening procedure every year
Ask the town to raise its dose each May
Let occupancy clear the water naturally each spring

nextClue.explanation: A documented opening flush with a residual check starts every season with fresh water proven at the far end.

clueText.nc-a: Opening day far end residual reads 0.7 mg/L after the flush and no stale complaints arrive that spring.
clueText.nc-b: The town entrance already delivers 0.85 mg/L on opening day.
clueText.nc-c: Natural clearing took two to three weeks of complaints, which the flush prevents.

tasks.prompt: One Ontario home has weak showers and slow filling appliances, but its garden hose fills a bucket at a normal rate outdoors.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional home with a pressure reducing valve on its service just inside the basement, installed 15 years ago. Street pressure is steady.

evidence.label: Static pressure at the outdoor tap, which is piped before the home reducing valve, is 420 kPa.
Pressure at an indoor tap downstream of the home reducing valve is 140 kPa and falls further when a second tap opens.
Bypassing the home reducing valve in a trial restores indoor pressure to near street pressure.
Both neighbours on the same service street have normal indoor pressure.
The home meter and strainer were cleaned last year and a recheck finds them clear.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The street main pressure has fallen for the whole block
The home meter strainer is blocked again
The home pressure reducing valve has failed and is over reducing indoor pressure
The home has a hidden leak that uses most of its flow

inference.explanation: Outdoor pressure before the valve is a healthy 420 kPa while indoor pressure after the valve is 140 kPa, the strainer is clear, and bypassing the valve restores indoor pressure. The failed home reducing valve is the only explanation consistent with all of these. A hidden leak would not be cured by bypassing the valve.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the home pressure reducing valve and set it to the recommended household pressure
Ask the utility to raise street pressure for the block
Replace the home meter again

nextClue.explanation: Replacing the failed reducing valve and setting it correctly is the direct fix, verified by indoor pressure returning to a normal controlled value.

clueText.nc-a: With the new valve set, indoor static pressure reads 350 kPa and showers run normally with two taps open.
clueText.nc-b: Street pressure is already 420 kPa at the outdoor tap, so the street is not the problem.
clueText.nc-c: The meter was rechecked clear, so replacing it again does not test the valve.

tasks.prompt: Loud banging shakes the discharge piping of an Ontario booster station each time a pump stops, and a pipe joint has begun to weep.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional booster station at the foot of a long rising main to an elevated tank. A surge relief and air valve sit at the station high point.

evidence.label: Pressure logging at the station shows a sharp spike to 900 kPa within a second of each pump stop, against a normal 450 kPa.
The bang and the spike occur only on pump stops, never on starts.
The high point air valve at the station is found with its isolating valve closed for maintenance done months earlier.
Check valves on both pumps were tested and close normally without slam when the air valve line is temporarily vented in a trial.
The weeping joint is on the discharge header near the station, where the spike is recorded.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The pump motors are oversized and start too fast
With the air valve isolated, pump stops send a pressure surge up the rising main that slams back at the station
The discharge header is undersized for normal pumping
The weeping joint is simply an old gasket failing with no pressure cause

inference.explanation: A 900 kPa spike timed to pump stops only, an air valve left isolated after maintenance, and normal behaviour in a vented trial point to surge on pump stop with no air cushion or venting path. Starts cause no bang, so motor starting is not the cause, and normal pumping at 450 kPa does not explain a weeping joint that tracks the spikes.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Return the air valve to service and repeat pressure logging through several pump stops
Slow every pump start with a longer ramp setting
Replace the weeping gasket and take no other action

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the air valve and logging pump stops directly tests whether the surge is controlled, which is the safety critical question.

clueText.nc-a: With the air valve in service, pump stop spikes fall to about 500 kPa and the banging stops, confirming surge control is restored.
clueText.nc-b: The spikes occur on stops, not starts, so a start ramp change does not address them.
clueText.nc-c: A new gasket alone would face the same 900 kPa spikes and likely weep again.

tasks.prompt: A new Ontario subdivision reports low pressure only at its farthest crescent, and only while lawn sprinklers run across the subdivision in the evening.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional subdivision fed through a pressure reducing valve station set at 310 kPa when the first phase was built. The crescent is the highest ground in the subdivision.

evidence.label: Evening logging shows the crescent at 170 kPa while the subdivision entrance holds 305 kPa.
The reducing valve station outlet gauge reads 310 kPa steady, matching its setpoint, during the same evenings.
Sprinkler demand across the subdivision triples total inflow on those evenings.
The crescent sits 18 m higher than the station, which alone accounts for about 175 kPa of static head difference.
On rainy evenings with sprinklers off, crescent pressure is an acceptable 260 kPa.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The reducing valve has failed closed and starves the subdivision
The crescent main is blocked by construction debris
Elevation head plus friction loss at sprinkler demand leaves the high crescent short, because the station setpoint was chosen for the low first phase
Residents on the crescent all have leaking services

inference.explanation: The station holds its 310 kPa setpoint, so it has not failed closed. The crescent is 18 m higher, worth about 175 kPa of head, and friction loss grows when sprinkler demand triples, which together explain why only the high crescent and only on sprinkler evenings falls short. Debris blockage or leaks would not follow the rain pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Log station outlet and crescent pressure together on a sprinkler evening to size a setpoint change for the higher ground
Excavate the crescent main to search for debris
Ban lawn sprinklers across the subdivision

nextClue.explanation: Paired logging sizes the actual elevation and friction loss, which is what a corrected setpoint or a small booster decision must be based on.

clueText.nc-a: Paired logs confirm about 135 kPa of combined elevation and friction loss at sprinkler peak, supporting a setpoint review for the station.
clueText.nc-b: Flow reaches the crescent and recovers fully on rainy evenings, so a debris blockage is not supported.
clueText.nc-c: A ban does not measure the loss and is not needed to confirm the hydraulics.

tasks.prompt: Pressure in one Ontario zone surges every time the tank fills at night: toilet valves fail and a relief valve at a school lifts repeatedly.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone where high lift pumps fill an elevated tank through the same main that feeds customers. Night filling is automatic.

evidence.label: Pressure loggers show zone pressure climbing to 700 kPa during the 01:00 to 03:00 fill window, against a normal 380 kPa.
The pressure rise begins and ends exactly with the fill pump run times in the station log.
The tank fill control valve, which should throttle as the tank nears full, is found stuck at full open with a broken actuator linkage.
Daytime pressures with pumps off are normal everywhere in the zone.
A supervised trial throttling the fill valve by hand holds zone pressure near 400 kPa through a full fill.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Night demand is so low that pressure naturally reaches 700 kPa
The tank fill valve stuck full open lets fill pumps push their full head into the zone main all night
The zone pressure reducing valve is set too high
Temperature changes at night expand the water and raise pressure

inference.explanation: The surge matches fill pump run times exactly, the fill valve is stuck full open with a broken linkage, and hand throttling holds normal pressure through a fill. Low night demand alone cannot push pressure to pump full head through a working throttling valve, and thermal expansion in an open distribution main does not create this pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Repair the fill valve actuator and log zone pressure through the next automatic fill
Tell customers to close their main shutoffs at night
Run the fill pumps only in daytime from now on

nextClue.explanation: Repairing the actuator and logging an automatic fill verifies the valve throttles again and the surge is gone under normal operation.

clueText.nc-a: After repair, the automatic fill peaks at 410 kPa in the zone and the school relief valve stays shut.
clueText.nc-b: Asking customers to shut off water nightly is unsafe and does not test the valve.
clueText.nc-c: Daytime filling would push the same uncontrolled head into a higher demand period.

tasks.prompt: Free chlorine holds at 0.9 mg/L leaving an Ontario plant and at mid system taps, but a group of streets beyond a ground level reservoir reads 0.1 mg/L or less.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional system with a ground level reservoir between the plant and the affected streets. Reservoir level and sampling records are available.

evidence.label: Samples at the reservoir inlet read 0.85 mg/L while samples at its outlet read 0.15 mg/L on the same day.
The reservoir level cycles only between 85 and 95 percent full, so most of its volume sits for many days.
Reservoir water temperature is 24 C and a sediment layer is visible through the inspection hatch.
Streets fed directly from the plant, bypassing the reservoir, hold 0.8 mg/L.
A trial that lowers the operating band and cycles the reservoir deeply raises outlet residual to 0.5 mg/L within days.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant chlorine dose has been cut without the operators knowing
The reservoir stores water so long, warm and over sediment, that residual is consumed before the water leaves
The affected streets have a large leak diluting the residual
The outlet sampling tap is contaminated and reads falsely low

inference.explanation: Residual falls across the reservoir itself, from 0.85 to 0.15 mg/L, while direct fed streets hold 0.8 mg/L on the same plant dose. Shallow level cycling, warm water, sediment, and recovery under deep cycling all point to storage decay in the reservoir. A leak cannot remove chlorine selectively, and a faulty tap cannot explain the trial recovery pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Set a deeper reservoir cycling range and schedule an interior cleaning inspection, then trend outlet residual daily
Double the plant chlorine dose for the whole system
Replace the reservoir outlet sampling tap and wait a month

nextClue.explanation: Deep cycling plus a cleaning inspection attacks the storage decay directly, and daily outlet trending verifies whether residual recovers and holds.

clueText.nc-a: Outlet residual climbs to 0.55 mg/L and holds for two weeks under deep cycling, confirming storage age and sediment demand were the cause.
clueText.nc-b: Doubling the plant dose would over chlorinate the direct fed streets that already hold 0.8 mg/L.
clueText.nc-c: The tap agreed with a second flushed sample, so replacing it does not test storage decay.

tasks.prompt: Chlorine residual is normal entering one Ontario street but nearly gone 400 m later, and the loss has grown worse over two summers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional street on an old unlined cast iron main. Paired sampling points bracket the street.

evidence.label: Paired same day samples read 0.8 mg/L at the street entrance and 0.1 mg/L at the far hydrant.
The street main is unlined cast iron with heavy internal rust tubercles confirmed on a repair coupon.
Flushing the street restores far end residual for about two days, then it decays again.
A parallel street on a newer lined main, with the same water age, holds 0.6 mg/L at its far end.
Iron in far end samples is elevated and the water there is slightly yellow after standing overnight.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Water age alone explains the loss, since the lined street loses residual the same way
The rough rusted interior of the old main exerts a high chlorine demand that consumes residual along the street
The far hydrant sample tap leaks and dilutes the sample
The plant dose falls every afternoon when the street is sampled

inference.explanation: The lined street with the same water age holds its residual, which rules out age alone. Heavy tuberculation on a repair coupon, elevated iron, and only two days of relief after flushing show the pipe wall demand consuming chlorine. A leaking sample tap would not raise iron or follow the flushing pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Collect paired entrance and far end residuals before and after a cleaning and lining assessment section to size the wall demand
Raise the plant dose until the far end reads 0.5 mg/L
Sample the far end only right after flushing from now on

nextClue.explanation: Paired sampling around a cleaned section measures how much of the loss is wall demand and whether rehabilitation restores residual.

clueText.nc-a: After the test section is cleaned, its far end residual rises from 0.1 to 0.55 mg/L at the same entrance residual, confirming wall demand.
clueText.nc-b: Raising the plant dose enough for this street would push the rest of the system far above target.
clueText.nc-c: Sampling only after flushing hides the normal condition instead of fixing it.

tasks.prompt: One Ontario pressure zone lost its chlorine residual over a weekend, while the rest of the system stayed normal, and Monday samples in the zone read zero.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with a booster chlorination station at its inlet that trims residual for the zone. Station logs are downloaded Monday.

evidence.label: Zone inlet samples upstream of the booster station read 0.7 mg/L all weekend.
The booster station hypochlorite tote is found empty on Monday, and its low level alarm had been silenced during Friday maintenance.
Station logs show the dosing pump ran all weekend against the empty tote.
Zone samples recover to 0.6 mg/L within a day of a fresh tote being connected and the pump primed.
Plant dose and all other zones held their normal residuals through the weekend.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A zone wide contamination event consumed all the chlorine
The booster chlorination station ran out of hypochlorite and dosed nothing all weekend after its alarm was silenced
The zone main developed a sudden large leak of chlorinated water
Weekend demand in the zone tripled and used up the residual

inference.explanation: Inlet water held 0.7 mg/L, the tote is empty, the pump ran dry with its alarm silenced, and residual recovered within a day of a fresh tote. That is a simple chemical outage. A contamination event large enough to zero a zone would show other quality changes, and neither a leak nor demand removes chlorine from water already in the mains.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Refill the tote, restore the low level alarm to active, and add a weekend tote level check to the station round
Flush the entire zone for two days to restore residual
Raise the plant dose to cover the zone permanently

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the alarm and adding a level check prevents a repeat silent outage, and zone trending verifies the booster is holding residual again.

clueText.nc-a: Zone residual holds at 0.6 mg/L through the next weekend with the alarm active and the tote checked on rounds.
clueText.nc-b: Flushing cannot add chlorine and the mains already receive 0.7 mg/L at the inlet.
clueText.nc-c: The plant already delivers target residual to the zone inlet, so a plant increase is not the fix.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario plant online chlorine analyzer shows 1.1 mg/L leaving the plant, yet distribution samples across town have fallen to 0.2 mg/L over a week.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant with an online analyzer on the treated water line and a bench DPD kit in the plant lab. Sampling is done by two methods.

evidence.label: Bench DPD tests at the plant outlet read 0.3 mg/L while the online analyzer beside them reads 1.1 mg/L.
The analyzer sample line is found partly plugged with scale, so it delivers old sample water slowly to the sensor.
Distribution bench samples agree with the plant bench result, not with the online analyzer.
Chlorine feed pump stroke and tote use match a low dose, not the dose the analyzer value would need.
After the sample line is cleaned and the analyzer calibrated, it reads 0.35 mg/L, matching the bench tests.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Distribution water age suddenly increased across the whole town
The online analyzer has been reading falsely high on stale sample water, so the plant has been under dosing for a week
Every bench DPD kit in town has failed at the same time
A town wide leak is diluting the distribution residual

inference.explanation: Two independent bench methods agree with each other and with the low chemical use, while only the online analyzer disagrees, and its sample line is plugged with scale. After cleaning and calibration it matches the bench. That is a false high analyzer masking under dosing, not a town wide change that would also have to fool the chemical feed records.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Clean and calibrate the analyzer, verify it against bench DPD daily for a week, and restore the dose to target
Trust the online analyzer and stop bench testing
Flush all town mains to raise the residual

nextClue.explanation: Daily analyzer versus bench comparison verifies the instrument now tracks the true residual while the corrected dose restores distribution values.

clueText.nc-a: Analyzer and bench readings agree within 0.05 mg/L for a week and distribution residual returns to 0.7 mg/L at the corrected dose.
clueText.nc-b: The bench tests, feed records, and distribution samples all contradicted the analyzer.
clueText.nc-c: Flushing does not add chlorine to water that is leaving the plant under dosed.

tasks.prompt: Residuals in an Ontario industrial park are acceptable Tuesday to Friday but fail every Monday morning, and the park manager wants the plant dose raised.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional industrial park loop fed from the town system. Most park businesses close on weekends.

evidence.label: Monday 08:00 samples at the park far end read 0.05 mg/L; by Tuesday noon the same tap reads 0.6 mg/L with no dose change.
Park water use meters show near zero demand from Friday evening to Monday morning.
The park loop is long and oversized for its weekday demand, and its far end warms to 22 C in summer.
Town samples at the park entrance read 0.8 mg/L every day including Mondays.
A Monday morning flush of the park loop restores far end residual within an hour, and complaints stop for that week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant lowers its dose every weekend
Weekend stagnation in the oversized park loop lets residual decay, and weekday use draws in fresh water again
A park tenant discharges chlorine consuming waste into the mains on Mondays
The Monday sampling officer uses a faulty test kit

inference.explanation: Entrance residual is normal on Mondays, park demand is near zero all weekend, and flushing or one day of weekday use restores the far end. That is weekend water age in an oversized loop. The plant dose is proven steady by the entrance samples, and a faulty kit would not be fixed by flushing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Set an automatic or scheduled Monday flush for the park loop and trend Monday residuals before considering any dose change
Raise the plant dose every Friday afternoon
Fine the park tenants for the Monday failures

nextClue.explanation: A scheduled Monday flush directly removes the aged weekend water, and trending shows whether Monday results pass without touching the plant dose.

clueText.nc-a: Monday far end samples pass at 0.5 mg/L for four straight weeks under the flush schedule.
clueText.nc-b: The entrance already reads 0.8 mg/L on Mondays, so the plant dose is not the gap.
clueText.nc-c: No tenant discharge was found, and weekday results pass with the same tenants present.
